author: Claude (English teacher role), v2 against the v2 quality gate
basis: Full rewrite. The workbook B1 column failed ten of twelve slides - semicolons and em-dashes that give a speaker no breathing cue, sentences of thirty words or more, and a long-word share at B2 level - and it sat 0.52 from the B2 text, which means the two levels were one text. This version keeps B1 grammar visible on purpose: present perfect on slides 1, 2, 8 and 10, a first conditional on slide 4, relative clauses on slides 1, 3, 7, 9, 11 and 12, and a because/so clause on slide 5. Meaning, slide order and every named fact are unchanged: SDG 9, the United Nations, ChatGPT, AI slop, the four parts of a prompt, literature review, lab report, presentation. Facts corrected: the workbook says the model 'only guesses the next word based on our prompt', which leaves out training, so slide 5 says it predicts from the words we typed and from the patterns in its training data. 'Natural intuition' becomes 'instinct' on slide 11 to stay inside the B1 lexical band; 'honest hearts' is kept as 'an honest heart'.

slides.1: Good morning. The United Nations has given us SDG 9, a goal that pushes every nation towards stronger industry, better networks and the research that keeps them alive.
slides.2: AI has already changed the pace of research and the way scientists talk to each other. But the quality of its answers depends on a single factor: how we phrase the question.
slides.3: As science undergraduates, we lean on ChatGPT almost weekly. It polishes a lab report, shortens a long article, or explains a concept that our lecture notes left unclear.
slides.4: Speed is not the problem. If we ask for something useful without supplying any detail, the reply will be vague and repetitive, and people now call that output AI slop.
slides.5: The system cannot guess our intentions. It predicts an answer from the words we typed and from the patterns in its training data, so a thin prompt produces a thin result.
slides.6: A strong prompt carries four things: a role for the model, the background it needs, a precise goal and a realistic limit. Clearer instructions reliably produce a more useful reply.
slides.7: In research, exact communication matters more than people think. A student who writes good prompts will produce a faster literature review, a tidier lab report and a clearer talk.
slides.8: However, if we take these answers without questioning them, we slowly turn into passive learners. Real science has always started with human curiosity, not with an easy click.
slides.9: So think carefully before you start typing. Decide precisely what information you need, ask who is going to read the answer, and choose the format that suits the task.
slides.10: Then hand over a clear set of instructions, including the background of your course and the exact format you expect. Writing a prompt has now become a real part of scientific communication.
slides.11: A computer can sort data very well, but it has no curiosity, no instinct and no honest heart. Those human traits are the ones that turn plain numbers into a discovery.
slides.12: Responsible innovation under SDG 9 starts with responsible talk. Better prompts will bring you better answers, but only a good scientist can turn those answers into knowledge that other people trust.
